Jeremiah Burroughs
jer-uh-MY-uh BUR-ohz
proper noun (person)
English Puritan preacher (1599-1646), Congregationalist, member of the Westminster Assembly, author of The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment.

📖 Biblical Definition

Jeremiah Burroughs was an English Puritan preacher and a member of the Westminster Assembly, best known for his classic treatise The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment, an exposition of Paul's words, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Phil 4:11). Burroughs defines Christian contentment as "that sweet, inward, quiet, gracious frame of spirit, which freely submits to and delights in God's wise and fatherly disposal in every condition." He distinguishes it sharply from stoic indifference and worldly resignation: it is not the absence of feeling but the presence of grace, a learned and supernatural calm that flows from trust in the sovereignty and goodness of God. Burroughs was famously irenic in a contentious age, laboring for peace among the godly; the motto often linked to him reads, "in necessary things, unity; in doubtful things, liberty; in all things, charity." His other works include Gospel Worship and The Evil of Evils, on the sinfulness of sin. Burroughs stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan teacher of contentment — not as passive fatalism, but as the soul's restful submission to and delight in the providence of a wise and fatherly God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Puritan preacher (1599-1646) and Westminster divine, author of The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment on Philippians 4:11; teacher of contentment as the soul's restful delight in God's fatherly providence, and a famously irenic peacemaker.

JEREMIAH BURROUGHS, proper noun. English Puritan preacher (1599-1646), member of the Westminster Assembly.

Author of The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment (on Phil 4:11).

Defined contentment as the soul's quiet, gracious submission to and delight in God's disposal.

Distinguished true contentment from stoic indifference and worldly resignation.

A famously irenic peacemaker; author also of Gospel Worship and The Evil of Evils.

📖 Key Scripture

Phil 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

Phil 4:12 — "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."

1 Tim 6:6 — "But godliness with contentment is great gain."

Heb 13:5 — "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Burroughs's teaching is corrupted when contentment is confused with stoic apathy or prosperity-driven striving, or when the Puritans are caricatured as gloomy when in fact they prized a deep and settled joy.

expand to see more

Stoicism-confused misreading. Some mistake Christian contentment for the Stoic's suppression of feeling or the fatalist's grim resignation. Burroughs labors to distinguish them: true contentment is not numbness but a gracious, supernatural restfulness that submits to and delights in God's fatherly will. The dictionary holds the difference — the believer is not steeled against providence but melted by trust in the God who orders it, content because the hand that disposes is a Father's.

Joyless-Puritan caricature. The modern myth of the gloomy Puritan collapses before Burroughs, who called contentment a "rare jewel" and made the pursuit of settled joy in God his life's theme. The dictionary recovers the truth that the Puritans were physicians of the soul who prescribed deep and durable gladness in God, against both the discontent of the flesh and the false cheer of the world.
